title: Comparatives & Superlatives
keyIdea: A comparative compares two things: taller than, more careful than. A superlative picks one out of three or more: the tallest, the most careful. Short words (one syllable) add -er and -est: fast, faster, fastest. Long words (three syllables or more) use more and most: more beautiful, most beautiful. Two-syllable words ending in y change y to i: happier, happiest. A few words break the rule: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst. Adverbs ending in -ly use more and most: more carefully. Never use both: more taller is wrong.
familyTip: Line up three things from the kitchen, like a cup, a jug and a bottle. Your child compares two (the jug is taller than the cup) and then picks out one (the bottle is the tallest). Swap in long words too: which is the most colourful? Listen for gooder or more bigger, and ask which one word does the job.

visual.caption: Does each word add -er, use more, or break the rule? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: compare towers, choose -er or more by syllables, fill the rule-breakers, pick adverb forms and delete the extra word in more taller.

kid: When you compare two things, add -er and use than. A giraffe is taller than a horse.
When you pick one out of a group, use the and add -est. The giraffe is the tallest animal.
Long words do not take -er. Say beautiful. It has three beats. So say more beautiful and the most beautiful. Words that end in y change y to i: happy, happier, happiest.
Some words break the rule: good, better, best and bad, worse, worst. Only use one way to compare. more taller is wrong; taller is enough.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. In England, adding -er and -est to adjectives (grander, fastest) is taught in Year 1 and Year 2 spelling (English Appendix 1). Common Core L.3.1g asks children to form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, and to choose between them. A comparative compares two things, usually with than. A superlative picks one out of three or more, usually with the.

Syllables decide the form. One-syllable adjectives take -er and -est, with spelling changes: drop the e (large, larger) or double the last letter after one short vowel (big, bigger). Two-syllable words that end in y change y to i (happy, happier). Most other two-syllable words (careful, famous) and all longer ones take more and most. A few take either (clever, quiet). Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; many, more, most; far, further, furthest.

Adverbs that end in -ly take more and most (more carefully). Short adverbs such as fast, hard and early take -er and -est, and well becomes better and best. Common mistakes: comparing twice (more taller, most biggest), regular endings on irregular words (gooder, baddest), -er on long words (beautifuller), more on short words (more fast), the superlative for just two things, and spelling slips (biger, happyer).

In the lab your child fills sentences about two or three towers, sorts eight adjectives by syllables into -er or more, fills five rule-breaker rows, picks the right adverb form in five sentences, and deletes the extra word in four double comparisons.

practice.prompt: There are two dogs. Rex is ___ than Max.
practice.hint: Two things, and the word than. Add -er, and only use one way to compare.
practice.explain: Two dogs, so use the comparative: bigger than. biggest is for three or more, and more bigger compares twice.

practice.prompt: There are {n} runners in a race. Ella is the fastest. How many runners is Ella faster than?
practice.hint: The fastest is faster than every other runner. Do not count Ella herself.
practice.explain: Ella is faster than all {n} runners except herself, so {=n-1} runners. That is what the superlative fastest means.

practice.hint: Clap famous. How many beats? Is it a word like happy that ends in y?
practice.explain: famous has two beats and does not end in y, so use more: more famous. famouser is not a word, and most famouser compares twice.

practice.prompt: Ann is {a} cm tall. Ben is {b} cm taller than Ann. How tall is Ben?
practice.hint: taller than Ann means Ann's height plus the extra.
practice.explain: Ben is {a} + {b} = {=a+b} cm tall. taller than compares the two heights.

practice.prompt: My drawing is good. Yours is ___.
practice.hint: good breaks the rule. It changes into a new word.
practice.explain: good, better, best. gooder and more good are not used.

pool.prompt: Of all the planets, Jupiter is the ___.
pool.hint: All the planets is a group, so use the and -est. big has one beat.
pool.explain: biggest picks one out of the group, and big doubles its g before -est. bigger compares only two, and most big uses most on a short word.

pool.hint: happy ends in y. What happens to the y before -est?
pool.explain: Change y to i, then add -est: happiest. happyest keeps the y, and most happyest compares twice.

pool.hint: loudly ends in -ly. -ly adverbs use more.
pool.explain: loudly is an -ly adverb, so use more: more loudly. loudlier is not a word, and more loudlier compares twice.

pool.prompt: Today's weather is bad. Yesterday's was even ___.
pool.hint: bad breaks the rule, like good does.
pool.explain: bad, worse, worst. badder and more bad are not standard English.

choices: This box is heavier than that one.
This box is more heavier than that one.
This box is the heaviest than that one.
pool.hint: Two boxes and the word than. Use one way to compare.
pool.explain: heavier than compares two boxes. more heavier compares twice, and the heaviest is for a group, not with than.

pool.prompt: A tower has {n} floors. The tallest tower in town has {d} more floors. How many floors does the tallest tower have?
pool.explain: {n} + {d} = {=n+d} floors. It is the tallest, so no tower in town has more.

pool.hint: hard is a short adverb. Short adverbs add -er.
pool.explain: hard takes -er: hard, harder. more harder compares twice, and hardlier is not a word.

pool.prompt: That was the ___ film I have ever seen.
pool.hint: exciting has three beats, and ever seen means out of all the films.
pool.explain: exciting is a long word, so use most for the superlative: the most exciting. more exciting compares only two.

pool.prompt: In a class, {n} children each made a paper plane. Only one plane flew the furthest. How many planes did it beat?
pool.hint: The furthest beat every other plane, but not itself.
pool.explain: It beat all {n} planes except itself: {=n-1} planes. furthest is the superlative of far.
